M7-01-FCFFFCFE.2: In {B_FCFF} compute FCFF (Free Cash Flow to Firm), the cash flow available to ALL capital providers (debt and equity together), BEFORE debt service: start from EBIT ({B_EBIT}) taxed at the tax rate ({B_ALIQ}), add back D&A ({B_DA}, a non-cash cost to add back), subtract Capex ({B_CAPEX}, a cash outflow that doesn't go through the income statement) and subtract ΔNWC ({B_DNWC}, already correctly signed: if positive it absorbed cash and is subtracted, if negative it released cash and subtracting it gives it back — the same sign already seen in M3-03).
M7-01-FCFFFCFE.3: In {B_FCFE} compute FCFE (Free Cash Flow to Equity), the flow left for shareholders ONLY: start from the FCFF just calculated ({B_FCFF} — DON'T recompute it from scratch), subtract net interest expense net of the tax shield ({B_INT} taxed at the rate {B_ALIQ}: it's already a cost deducted in the income statement, so it's taxed "less" like EBIT before subtracting it) and subtract the year's net debt repayment ({B_RIMB}, cash paid out to debt providers, not available to shareholders). CAREFUL: FCFE will be discounted at the cost of equity (Ke), NEVER at the WACC — the WACC is an average with the cost of debt, which is lower, and would use a rate too light for the true risk of a flow belonging only to equity, overstating its value. You're not discounting anything yet here: the point is to learn it for the levels that follow.
M7-01-FCFFFCFE.4:
## FCFF vs FCFE: two flows, two discount rates

A DCF valuation discounts a future cash flow. But "the" cash flow isn't just one: there are two versions, and using the wrong one with the wrong rate is the most common mistake of anyone starting to build a DCF.

- **FCFF (Free Cash Flow to Firm)**: the flow available to ALL of the company's capital providers, debt AND equity together, calculated BEFORE paying interest or repaying debt. It's discounted at the **WACC**, the weighted average cost of all sources of capital (you'll build it in the next levels of this module).
- **FCFE (Free Cash Flow to Equity)**: the flow left for shareholders ONLY, after the debt has been serviced (interest paid, principal repaid or raised). It's discounted at the **cost of equity (Ke)**.

> **FCFF = EBIT × (1 − tax rate) + D&A − Capex − ΔNWC**
> **FCFE = FCFF − Net interest expense × (1 − tax rate) − Net debt repayment**

**The mistake never to make**: discounting FCFE at the WACC. The WACC is an average between the cost of debt (lower, debt is less risky for the lender) and the cost of equity (higher). FCFE belongs ONLY to shareholders: its risk is that of levered equity, not an average with debt. Discounting it at the WACC would use a rate too low for its true risk, and equity value would come out OVERSTATED. In this level you don't discount anything yet — the point is to fix the distinction before getting to the WACC and Ke in the following levels.

The year's data: EBIT {p0}, tax rate {p1} (Italian corporate tax, IRES, fixed by law), depreciation (D&A) {p2}, Capex {p3}, ΔNWC {p4}, net interest expense {p5}, net debt repayment for the year {p6}.

First compute FCFF, then use it to get to FCFE. The second task is NOT recomputed from scratch: it starts from the result of the first.

M7-02-COSTRUZIONEFCF.2: In {B_EBIT} compute the year's EBIT: EBITDA ({B_EBITDA}) minus D&A ({B_DA}). EBITDA is the operating margin BEFORE depreciation and taxes; subtracting D&A gets you to EBIT, the operating margin after accounting for the wear of assets — but still before taxes.
M7-02-COSTRUZIONEFCF.3: In {B_NOPAT} compute NOPAT (Net Operating Profit After Tax, EBIT after taxes): the EBIT just calculated ({B_EBIT} — DON'T recompute it from scratch) times (1 - tax rate), with the rate in {B_ALIQ}.
M7-02-COSTRUZIONEFCF.4: In {B_FCFF} compute FCFF (Free Cash Flow to Firm): start from the NOPAT just calculated ({B_NOPAT} — DON'T recompute it from scratch), ADD BACK D&A ({B_DA}), subtract Capex ({B_CAPEX}) and subtract ΔNWC ({B_DNWC}, already correctly signed). Why add back D&A after already subtracting it to get to EBIT and NOPAT? Because it's a NON-cash cost: it reduces taxable income (rightly, it's a real cost in the income statement) but it's never an actual cash outflow — no bank transfer goes out when depreciation is booked. NOPAT has already benefited from the D&A tax shield, but it's still an "income statement" number, not a cash number: adding back D&A is the step that turns it back into a real cash flow.
M7-02-COSTRUZIONEFCF.5:
## Building FCF, line by line

In the previous level EBIT was already given. In a real model it never is: it comes from a projected income statement starting from EBITDA and D&A, two separate lines. Here you build FCFF from scratch, starting exactly there.

> **EBIT = EBITDA − D&A**
> **NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − tax rate)**
> **FCFF = NOPAT + D&A − Capex − ΔNWC**

**Why D&A appears twice, first subtracted and then added back**: it's a non-cash cost. It reduces taxable income — rightly, it's a real cost — but no cash ever leaves when depreciation is booked. NOPAT is an income statement number, already corrected for taxes but not yet for real cash: adding back D&A is the step that turns it into a cash flow.

The year's data: EBITDA {p0}, depreciation (D&A) {p1}, tax rate {p2} (Italian corporate tax, IRES, fixed by law), Capex {p3}, ΔNWC {p4}.

Three tasks in sequence: EBIT, then NOPAT, then FCFF. Each task uses the result of the previous one — never recompute it from scratch.

M7-03-MIDYEARSTUB.7:
## Mid-year convention and stub period

The textbook formula discounts every annual flow as if it all arrived on 31/12: exponent -1, -2, -3... In reality a company collects and pays throughout the WHOLE year, not in one go at year end. On average, an evenly spread flow arrives HALFWAY through its period: that's the **mid-year convention**, and it changes the exponent from -1 to -0.5 for the first full year. Discounting for LESS time INCREASES present value — a euro in 6 months is worth more than a euro in 12.

There's a second complication, almost always present in a real DCF: the valuation date hardly ever falls exactly at the start of the company's fiscal year. The first period actually discounted isn't a full year: it's the **stub period**, the piece of fiscal year left from the valuation date to its end — shorter than 12 months. The mid-year convention applies to HALF of THIS shorter period, not half of a whole year.

The first full fiscal year starts at the end of the stub: its flow arrives on average at stub + half a year from the valuation date. The textbooks' -0.5 exponent holds only when valuing exactly at the start of the fiscal year; each following year adds 1.

Data: WACC {p0} (given, it's not the subject of this level). Valuation date {p1}/{p2}/{p3}. End of the first fiscal year {p4}/{p5}/{p6} — {p7} days later.

Three tasks: the stub fraction, the stub discount factor, the first full year's factor. The last two reference the stub fraction: never recompute it from scratch.

M7-04-CAPM.2: In {B_KE} compute the cost of equity (Ke) with the CAPM: the risk-free rate ({B_RF}) plus beta ({B_BETA}) times the equity risk premium ({B_ERP}). Formula: Ke = Rf + beta × ERP. Beta measures this company's SYSTEMATIC risk relative to the market: a beta above 1 means a stock more volatile than the market (it amplifies its moves, so higher systematic risk and a higher Ke), a beta below 1 the opposite — a more defensive stock, moving less than the market, with a lower Ke. Use the three given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-04-CAPM.3: The value is off: check that you're adding the risk-free rate and multiplying beta by the ERP, not some other combination of the three cells.
M7-04-CAPM.4:
## CAPM: the cost of equity

The WACC (the rate FCFF is discounted at, M7-07) is a weighted average between the cost of debt and the cost of equity (Ke). The CAPM (Capital Asset Pricing Model) is the standard way to estimate Ke.

> **Ke = Rf + beta × ERP**

- **Rf (risk-free rate)**: the return on a risk-free investment, typically a long-dated government bond.
- **ERP (equity risk premium)**: the EXTRA return the stock market as a whole demands over the risk-free rate, to accept the risk of holding shares.
- **beta**: this company's SYSTEMATIC risk, relative to the market. beta = 1 means "moves like the market"; **beta > 1** means a stock **more volatile** than the market — it amplifies its moves, so the market demands a **higher** Ke to compensate for the greater risk; **beta < 1** means the opposite, a **more defensive** stock and a **lower** Ke.

Beta multiplies the ERP: the ERP is a market figure that's the same for all companies listed on the same market, beta scales it to the specific risk of THIS company. The result, added to the risk-free rate, is the total expected return demanded by those holding this company's equity.

**The data**, already set as market assumptions: risk-free rate {p0}, beta {p1}, equity risk premium {p2}.
M7-04-CAPM.11: ={B_RF}+{B_BETA}*{B_ERP}: risk-free rate plus beta times the ERP (here it's {p3}).
M7-04-CAPM.title: CAPM: the cost of equity
M7-05-BETAHAMADA.2: In {B_BETA_UNLEV} compute the peer's UNLEVERED beta: remove the effect of THE PEER'S financial leverage from its observed levered beta ({B_BETA_PEER}), using the peer's D/E ({B_DE_PEER}) and the tax rate ({B_TAX}). Hamada formula (unlever): Unlevered beta = Levered beta / (1 + (1 - tax rate) × D/E). The unlevered beta is the business's "pure" beta — the one the company would have if it were financed only with equity, no debt — independent of how the specific peer is financed. It's an INTERMEDIATE result: it's not yet the beta to use in the CAPM of the company being valued (that comes in T2). Use the three given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-05-BETAHAMADA.3: The value is off: check that you're DIVIDING the levered beta by (1 + (1 - tax rate) × the peer's D/E), not multiplying, or using the tax rate on its own instead of (1 - tax rate).
M7-05-BETAHAMADA.4: In {B_BETA_RELEV} compute the beta RELEVERED to the TARGET structure: start again from the unlevered beta just calculated ({B_BETA_UNLEV}) and apply the TARGET leverage of the company being valued ({B_DE_TARGET}), with the same tax rate ({B_TAX}). Hamada formula (relever): Relevered beta = Unlevered beta × (1 + (1 - tax rate) × target D/E). Careful: the leverage to use here is the TARGET one, NOT the peer's ({B_DE_PEER} has already been used and "consumed" in T1) — the whole point of the exercise is to dress the business's pure beta in the capital structure OF THE COMPANY BEING VALUED, not in that of the peer it started from. Use the three given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-05-BETAHAMADA.5: The value is off: check that you're MULTIPLYING the unlevered beta by (1 + (1 - tax rate) × TARGET D/E) — use the target leverage, not the peer's.
M7-05-BETAHAMADA.6:
## Hamada beta: unlevering and relevering a peer's beta

The CAPM (M7-04) needs a beta, but a listed peer's observed beta CAN'T be reused as it is: that beta also reflects THAT peer's capital structure (the Debt/Equity ratio, "D/E"), not that of the company you're valuing. The more indebted a company, the more risk is amplified for equity holders — so the observed levered beta "contains" a piece of risk that depends on how much debt the peer has, not only on the risk of the business itself.

The Hamada formula separates the two things in two steps, in this order:

**1) Unlever — remove THE PEER'S leverage:**

> **Unlevered beta = Peer levered beta / (1 + (1 - tax rate) × peer D/E)**

The unlevered beta is the business's "pure" beta: the one the company would have if it were financed only with equity, no debt. It's an INTERMEDIATE result, never the final number to use in the CAPM.

**2) Relever — apply the TARGET leverage:**

> **Relevered beta = Unlevered beta × (1 + (1 - tax rate) × target D/E)**

Here you apply the TARGET D/E — that of the company being valued, not the peer's — to get the beta reflecting ITS risk.

The tax rate comes in because interest on debt is deductible: the tax shield reduces the effect of leverage on equity risk, which is why it appears as (1 - tax rate) and not on its own.

**The data**, already set as assumptions: comparable peer's levered beta {p0}, peer D/E {p1}x, tax rate {p2}, target D/E of the company being valued {p3}x.
M7-05-BETAHAMADA.15: ={B_BETA_PEER}/(1+(1-{B_TAX})*{B_DE_PEER}): peer levered beta divided by (1 + (1 - tax rate) × peer D/E) (here it's {p3}).
M7-05-BETAHAMADA.16: ={B_BETA_UNLEV}*(1+(1-{B_TAX})*{B_DE_TARGET}): unlevered beta times (1 + (1 - tax rate) × TARGET D/E) (here it's {p3}).
M7-05-BETAHAMADA.title: Hamada beta: unlevering and relevering a peer's beta
M7-06-COUNTRYRISK.2: In {B_KE_ADJ} compute the cost of equity adjusted for country risk: base Ke from the CAPM ({B_KE_BASE}) PLUS the country risk premium ({B_CRP}). Formula: Adjusted Ke = Base Ke + CRP. The CRP is an addend, not a multiplier: it's a premium for an ADDITIONAL risk (the sovereign risk of the country the company operates in) beyond what beta already captures in base Ke (the company's specific systematic risk). For Italy, the typical CRP is the BTP-Bund spread: a measurable spread of Italian sovereign debt over the German risk-free benchmark. Use the two given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-06-COUNTRYRISK.3: The value is off: check that you're ADDING base Ke and the country risk premium, not multiplying them or combining them some other way.
M7-06-COUNTRYRISK.4:
## Country risk premium: Ke adjusted for country risk

The CAPM of M7-04 estimates Ke from Rf, beta and ERP — but those figures are typically observed against a "pure risk-free" benchmark (e.g. the German Bund for the euro area). If the company operates in a market whose sovereign debt pays a measurable spread over that benchmark — Italy, with the BTP-Bund spread, is the classic example — that estimate is incomplete: it's missing the COUNTRY's risk, not just the company's.

> **Adjusted Ke = Base Ke + CRP**

- **Base Ke**: the cost of equity from the CAPM (M7-04), calculated on a "pure" risk-free benchmark.
- **CRP (country risk premium)**: the country's sovereign debt spread over that risk-free benchmark — for Italy, the BTP-Bund spread.

The CRP is ADDED to base Ke, it doesn't multiply it: it's an ADDITIONAL premium for a risk of a different nature (the country's risk) from what beta already captures in base Ke (the company's specific systematic risk, relative to its market). It isn't a universal addend: it makes sense when the country in question has a measurable sovereign spread — it shouldn't be added regardless to every Ke, of every company, in every country.

**The data**, already set as assumptions: base Ke from the CAPM {p0}, Italy country risk premium (BTP-Bund spread) {p1}.
M7-06-COUNTRYRISK.10: ={B_KE_BASE}+{B_CRP}: base Ke plus the country risk premium, no multiplying (here it's {p2}).
M7-06-COUNTRYRISK.title: Country risk premium: Ke adjusted for country risk
M7-07-WACC.2: In {B_KD_AT} compute the AFTER-tax cost of debt: the pre-tax cost of debt ({B_KD}) times (1 - tax rate) ({B_TAX}). Formula: After-tax Kd = Kd × (1 - tax rate). Interest on debt is tax-deductible: paying it reduces taxable profit, and so reduces the taxes owed. The company's "true" cost of debt is therefore lower than the nominal rate it pays creditors — this is the tax shield. Use the two given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-07-WACC.3: The value is off: check that you're multiplying Kd by (1 - tax rate), not by the tax rate alone (and not by (1 + tax rate)).
M7-07-WACC.4: In {B_WACC} compute the WACC: the weighted average of the cost of equity ({B_KE}) weighted by the equity weight ({B_WE}) and the AFTER-tax cost of debt just calculated in T1 ({B_KD_AT}) weighted by the debt weight ({B_WD}). Formula: WACC = Ke × equity weight + after-tax Kd × debt weight. IMPORTANT: use {B_KD_AT} (the AFTER-tax cost of debt, calculated in T1), NOT {B_KD} (the nominal PRE-tax Kd) — the tax shield on interest reduces the company's effective cost of debt, and the WACC must weight that true cost, not the gross one. Ke, on the other hand, goes in unadjusted: dividends paid to shareholders aren't deductible, so equity has no equivalent tax shield. Use the four given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-07-WACC.5: The value is off: check that you're using the AFTER-tax cost of debt ({B_KD_AT}, from T1) and not pre-tax Kd ({B_KD}) directly, and that you're weighting Ke by the equity weight and after-tax Kd by the debt weight (not the other way round).
M7-07-WACC.6:
## WACC: the weighted average cost of capital

FCFF is discounted at the WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital): the average cost of ALL the capital financing the company, not just equity. It's a weighted average between the cost of equity (Ke, already available from M7-06) and the cost of debt — but debt goes in AFTER a tax adjustment.

**Why debt costs LESS than its nominal rate.** Interest on debt is tax-deductible: paying it reduces taxable profit, and so reduces the taxes owed. The company's "true" cost of debt isn't the rate Kd it pays creditors, but that rate net of this tax shield:

> **After-tax Kd = Kd × (1 - tax rate)**

Ke has no equivalent: dividends paid to shareholders aren't deductible, so equity generates no tax shield. That's why the WACC weights Ke gross, but debt only AFTER cleaning it up:

> **WACC = Ke × equity weight + after-tax Kd × debt weight**

The weights (E/(D+E) and D/(D+E), which always add up to 1) are the company's TARGET capital structure — how much of the total capital is financed by equity versus debt.

**The data**, already set as assumptions: Ke adjusted for country risk (M7-06) {p0}, pre-tax cost of debt (Kd) {p1}, tax rate {p2}, target equity weight E/(D+E) {p3}, target debt weight D/(D+E) {p4}.
M7-07-WACC.7: WACC: the weighted average cost of capital

M7-07-WACC.16: ={B_KE}*{B_WE}+{B_KD_AT}*{B_WD}: Ke times the equity weight, plus after-tax Kd (not pre-tax Kd) times the debt weight (here it's {p4}).
M7-07-WACC.title: WACC: the weighted average cost of capital
M7-08-STRUTTURATARGET.2: In {B_WACC_ATTUALE} compute the WACC using the CURRENT (post-LBO) capital structure: Ke ({B_KE}) weighted by (1 - current debt weight) plus after-tax Kd ({B_KD_AT}) weighted by the current debt weight ({B_WD_ATTUALE}). Formula: WACC(current) = Ke × (1 - current debt weight) + after-tax Kd × current debt weight. This is the WACC you'd get using the company's leverage TODAY — much higher than its long-term structure because it has just come out of an LBO — and it's calculated here to be compared with the correct one in T2, but it is NOT the right one to discount a DCF's flows. Use the three given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.

M7-08-STRUTTURATARGET.4: In {B_WACC_TARGET} compute the WACC using the TARGET (long-term) capital structure: Ke ({B_KE}) weighted by (1 - target debt weight) plus after-tax Kd ({B_KD_AT}) weighted by the target debt weight ({B_WD_TARGET}). Formula: WACC(target) = Ke × (1 - target debt weight) + after-tax Kd × target debt weight. IMPORTANT: use {B_WD_TARGET} (the TARGET, long-term debt weight), NOT {B_WD_ATTUALE} (the current debt weight, already used in T1) — Ke and after-tax Kd are the same as T1 (they don't change in this simplified exercise), ONLY the capital structure weighting them changes. This IS the right WACC to discount a DCF's flows, because it represents the leverage the company will have for most of its life, not a temporary state. Use the three given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-08-STRUTTURATARGET.5: The value is off: check that you're using the TARGET debt weight ({B_WD_TARGET}), not the current one ({B_WD_ATTUALE}), and that you're weighting Ke by (1 - target debt weight) and after-tax Kd by the target debt weight (not the other way round).
M7-08-STRUTTURATARGET.6: In {B_DIFF_BPS} compute the difference between the two WACCs, in basis points (1 basis point = 0.01%): target WACC ({B_WACC_TARGET}) minus current WACC ({B_WACC_ATTUALE}), times 10,000 to convert the difference from a fraction to basis points. Formula: difference in bps = (WACC(target) - WACC(current)) × 10,000. WATCH the order of subtraction: TARGET minus CURRENT ({B_WACC_TARGET} - {B_WACC_ATTUALE}), not the other way round — a flipped sign here gives no error, just a number with the wrong sign, the easiest kind of bug to miss. Even a few dozen basis points of WACC, over a valuation horizon as long as a DCF's, move the present value of the discounted flows far from negligibly: it's the concrete measure of what using the wrong leverage costs. Use the two given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-08-STRUTTURATARGET.7: The value is off: check the order of subtraction (target WACC minus current WACC, i.e. {B_WACC_TARGET} - {B_WACC_ATTUALE}, not the other way round) and that you're multiplying by 10,000 (not by 100, which would give percentage points, not basis points).
M7-08-STRUTTURATARGET.8:
## Capital structure: current vs target in the WACC

A company that has just been through an LBO (leveraged buyout) is often indebted FAR beyond what its long-term setup will be: the business plan foresees deleveraging (progressive debt reduction) towards a "target" structure — often close to the sector average — over a few years.

**The DCF's WACC must use LONG-term leverage, not today's.** The WACC discounting a DCF's cash flows must represent the "steady-state" cost of capital: the financial structure the company will have for most of its life, not a temporary state. Using the CURRENT weights of a company just loaded with LBO debt means giving debt (cheaper than equity) an ARTIFICIALLY high weight — this lowers the calculated WACC, and so RAISES the present value of the discounted flows: an error that systematically overstates the valuation.

> **WACC = Ke × (1 - debt weight) + after-tax Kd × debt weight**

This level isolates the effect of the WEIGHTS with everything else equal: same Ke, same after-tax Kd, two different capital structures (current and target), two different WACCs.

*Stated simplification:* in reality Ke would also change with leverage (beta would have to be relevered with the Hamada formula, as in M7-05, at the NEW leverage) — here Ke is kept constant on purpose, to isolate the effect of the weights without recalculating the whole chain.

**The data**, already set as assumptions: CURRENT debt weight D/(D+E) (post-LBO) {p0}, TARGET debt weight D/(D+E) (long-term structure) {p1}, Ke {p2}, after-tax Kd {p3}.

M7-09-GORDONGROWTH.2: In {B_FCF1} compute the normalised FCF of the FIRST year of the perpetuity: the FCF of the last explicit year ({B_FCF}) times (1 + g), with g in {B_G}. Formula: FCF(first perpetuity year) = FCF(last explicit year) × (1 + g). The first flow of the perpetuity you're about to discount is NOT the last explicit year's FCF: it arrives one year LATER, so it has already grown by one period at rate g. Use the two given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-09-GORDONGROWTH.3: In {B_TV} compute the Terminal Value with the Gordon growth method: the normalised first-perpetuity-year FCF just calculated in T1 ({B_FCF1} — DON'T recompute it from scratch) divided by (WACC - g), with WACC in {B_WACC} and g in {B_G}. Formula: Terminal Value = {B_FCF1} / ({B_WACC} - {B_G}). WATCH the order of subtraction in the denominator: WACC MINUS g ({B_WACC} - {B_G}), never the other way round — flipping it flips the sign of the terminal value, and a company can't be worth a negative amount. Use the three given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-09-GORDONGROWTH.4: The value is off: check that you're dividing by (WACC - g) and not by (g - WACC), and that the numerator is {B_FCF1} (the FCF already grown in T1), not the last explicit year's FCF taken directly.
M7-09-GORDONGROWTH.5:
## Terminal value: the Gordon growth method

A DCF explicitly discounts only a finite number of years. Beyond that horizon, the company's residual value is compressed into a SINGLE number, the **terminal value** — which usually makes up the majority of total present value.

**The most common method, Gordon growth**, assumes that beyond the last explicit year FCF keeps growing forever at a CONSTANT, low rate g — the growth of a mature economy, never that of a hyper-growth company: no company grows faster than nominal GDP forever. The present value of this growing perpetuity is:

> **Terminal Value = FCF(first perpetuity year) / (WACC − g)**

**Which FCF goes in the numerator, and why.** The first flow of the perpetuity is NOT the last explicit year's FCF: it arrives one year LATER, so it has already grown by one period at rate g:

> **FCF(first perpetuity year) = FCF(last explicit year) × (1 + g)**

Using the last explicit year's FCF directly, without growing it, would SYSTEMATICALLY understate the terminal value: an apparently small error that applies to the whole perpetuity, propagating in full into the number that usually weighs more than half the valuation.

*The constraint that holds the formula together:* **WACC must always stay significantly above g.** If the two got close, the denominator would collapse towards zero and the terminal value would explode; if WACC fell below g, the denominator would turn negative and the result would lose all economic meaning — a company can't be worth a negative amount.

**The data**, already set as assumptions: FCF of the projection's last explicit year {p0}, perpetual growth rate g {p1}, WACC {p2}.

M7-10-EXITMULTIPLE.2: In {B_TV_EXIT} compute the Terminal Value with the exit multiple method: the last explicit year's EBITDA ({B_EBITDA}) times the market exit multiple ({B_MULT_MKT}). Formula: Terminal Value (exit multiple) = EBITDA(last explicit year) × exit multiple. Unlike Gordon growth, this method doesn't project a perpetuity: it assumes that, at the end of the explicit horizon, the company is sold at a market multiple observable today. Use the two given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-10-EXITMULTIPLE.3: In {B_MULT_IMPLICITO} compute the multiple IMPLIED by the Terminal Value obtained with the Gordon growth method ({B_TV_GORDON}, given — the conceptual result of M7-09): divide it by the last explicit year's EBITDA ({B_EBITDA}). Formula: implied multiple (Gordon) = TV(Gordon growth) / EBITDA(last explicit year). It's the question "what EBITDA multiple does the Terminal Value produced by the Gordon method essentially correspond to?" — the same unit of measure as the market multiple used in T1, needed for the comparison in the next task. Use the two given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-10-EXITMULTIPLE.4: In {B_SCOSTAMENTO} compute the % deviation between the Gordon implied multiple just calculated in T2 ({B_MULT_IMPLICITO} — DON'T recompute it from scratch) and the market multiple used in T1 ({B_MULT_MKT}): ({B_MULT_IMPLICITO}-{B_MULT_MKT})/{B_MULT_MKT}. WATCH the order: the Gordon implied multiple MINUS the market multiple, all divided by the market multiple (not by the implied one) — swapping numerator or denominator changes both the sign and the scale of the result. A positive result says Gordon implies a HIGHER multiple than the market's; negative, a LOWER one. If the deviation is large (roughly over 20%-30% in absolute value), it's a signal that the WACC and g assumptions used in Gordon need reviewing: the two methods should tell similar stories, not wildly different ones — an implied multiple that's too high usually comes from a g that's too optimistic or a WACC that's too compressed.
M7-10-EXITMULTIPLE.5: The value is off: check that the numerator is (Gordon implied multiple − market multiple), i.e. ({B_MULT_IMPLICITO}-{B_MULT_MKT}), and that you're dividing by the MARKET multiple ({B_MULT_MKT}), not by the implied one ({B_MULT_IMPLICITO}).
M7-10-EXITMULTIPLE.6:
## Terminal value: exit multiple and cross-check with Gordon

The second method, after Gordon growth (M7-09), to estimate a DCF's terminal value. The **exit multiple method** doesn't project a perpetuity: it assumes that, at the end of the explicit horizon, the company is sold at a market multiple observable TODAY on the last explicit year's EBITDA — the same multiple at which you'd negotiate a comparable transaction at that moment:

> **Terminal Value (exit multiple) = EBITDA(last explicit year) × exit multiple**

**The central point of this level: the cross-check.** Gordon growth and exit multiple are two different roads to the SAME conceptual number, and should tell compatible stories. The standard way to check isn't to compare the two Terminal Values directly in euros (the scales can differ for a thousand reasons), but to translate Gordon's TV into an IMPLIED EBITDA MULTIPLE — the same unit of measure as the exit multiple method:

> **Implied multiple (Gordon) = TV(Gordon growth) / EBITDA(last explicit year)**

If that implied multiple is close to the market multiple used for the exit multiple, the two methods confirm each other. If the deviation is large — roughly over 20%-30% — it's a signal that the WACC and g assumptions used in Gordon need reviewing, not that the exit multiple method is wrong: an implied multiple that's too high usually comes from a g that's too optimistic or a WACC that's too compressed.

**The data**, already set as assumptions: EBITDA of the projection's last explicit year {p0}, market exit multiple {p1}, Terminal Value with the Gordon growth method (M7-09, given) {p2}.

M7-11-CAPEXTERMINALE.2: In {B_CAPEX_NORM} compute the NORMALISED capex to use in the terminal value: the same convention as M3-04 (maintenance capex ≈ D&A), applied here to the "stylised" perpetuity year. In the long run a company in steady state can't keep expanding its productive capacity forever: capex must converge towards the last explicit year's D&A ({B_DA}). Use that cell directly as the estimate, without copying the number by hand.
M7-11-CAPEXTERMINALE.3: In {B_FCF_NORM} compute the normalised FCF for the terminal value: the last explicit year's FCF BEFORE normalisation ({B_FCF_PRIMA} — already calculated with raw capex, don't touch it) PLUS the difference between raw capex ({B_CAPEX_GREZZO}) and the normalised capex just calculated in T1 ({B_CAPEX_NORM} — DON'T recompute it from scratch). Formula: Normalised FCF = {B_FCF_PRIMA} + ({B_CAPEX_GREZZO} − {B_CAPEX_NORM}). The idea: that starting FCF had already subtracted RAW capex, higher than what steady state would need; this formula "gives back" exactly the excess slice of capex. WATCH the order of subtraction inside the brackets: raw capex MINUS normalised capex ({B_CAPEX_GREZZO} − {B_CAPEX_NORM}), never the other way round — flipping it would take cash away instead of giving it back, understating the terminal FCF even further instead of correcting it. Use the three given cells, without copying the numbers by hand.
M7-11-CAPEXTERMINALE.4:
## Normalising capex in the terminal value

M3-04 taught you to split a year's TOTAL capex into maintenance capex (proxy: converges towards D&A) and growth capex (the rest, discretionary). Here we pick up the SAME proxy — maintenance capex ≈ D&A — but for a different problem: normalising the last explicit year's capex before using it to build the terminal value (M7-09).

**Why it's needed.** Gordon growth (M7-09) assumes that beyond the last explicit year the company grows forever at a low, constant rate g — a steady state. But a company in steady state can't keep EXPANDING its productive capacity forever: in the long run capex must be limited to replacing what wears out, i.e. converge towards D&A. If instead you carried into the terminal value the RAW capex projected for the last explicit year — perhaps still high because an expansion project was still under way that year — the terminal FCF (and so the Terminal Value, which normally makes up most of the valuation) would be systematically UNDERSTATED.

> **Normalised capex (for the terminal value) = last explicit year's D&A**
> **Normalised FCF = FCF before normalisation + (Raw capex − Normalised capex)**

The FCF "before normalisation" has already been calculated by subtracting the higher RAW capex. To get the FCF you'd have had in steady state, you "give back" exactly the difference between the two capex figures: how much more was subtracted than should have been.

**The data**, already set as assumptions: raw capex of the last explicit year {p0}, D&A of the last explicit year {p1}, FCF of the last explicit year before normalisation {p2}.

First compute normalised capex, then use it to normalise FCF. This level stops here: the normalised FCF you get is the clean input that would go in the numerator of the Gordon formula (M7-09), you don't recalculate the Terminal Value itself here.

M7-12-NOL.2: In {B_NOLUSATO} compute the NOL ACTUALLY USED this year. It isn't simply the remaining NOL ({B_NOL}) nor simply taxable income before NOL ({B_REDD}): it's bound by TWO independent caps, and can't exceed EITHER of them. First cap: you can't use more tax credit than you actually have in {B_NOL}. Second cap: there's no point taking taxable income below zero — the NOL cuts taxes down to zero, it doesn't generate a refund, so you can't use more than {B_REDD}. The NOL used is therefore the SMALLER of the two: use the MIN function.
M7-12-NOL.3: In {B_IMPEFF} compute the TAXES ACTUALLY PAID this year: taxable income before NOL ({B_REDD}) MINUS the NOL just used ({B_NOLUSATO} — DON'T recompute it from scratch), times the IRES rate ({B_ALIQ}). Compare this number with what the company would pay WITHOUT the NOL, i.e. {B_REDD} times the rate alone: the difference between the two is the concrete value, in euros, of the NOL tax shield — the more remaining NOL you've used, the less tax you've paid.
M7-12-NOL.4:
## NOL: past tax losses are a credit, not just a memory

A company that accumulated tax losses in past years doesn't lose them: it can carry them forward and use them to reduce taxable income in future years. It's a real tax shield, to be valued in Free Cash Flow just like D&A or interest expense: it reduces the taxes ACTUALLY paid, not just those "on paper".

**Why you need a MIN and not a direct subtraction**: the NOL used in a year can NEVER exceed two independent caps — the remaining NOL you actually have available, and the year's taxable income (no point taking it below zero, the NOL doesn't generate a refund). The NOL used is the SMALLER of the two caps.

**Stated simplification**: in Italy (art. 84 TUIR) losses carried forward offset at most 80% of each year's income, except those from the first three financial years. Here the rule without a cap is used, the one in many international models.

The year's data: remaining NOL at the start of the year {p0}, taxable income before NOL {p1}, IRES rate {p2}. Without the NOL, the company would have paid {p3} in taxes: how much it saves thanks to the NOL you'll find out by calculating the two tasks below.

M7-12-NOL.8: Taxable income before NOL for the year, €

M7-12-NOL.14: =({B_REDD}-{B_NOLUSATO})*{B_ALIQ}: taxable income minus the NOL used, times the IRES rate.

M7-13-SENSITIVITY.8:
## The table that ends up in committee

Every DCF discounts a Terminal Value that depends on two assumptions nobody knows for
certain: the **WACC** (the cost of capital used to discount) and **g** (perpetual
growth beyond the explicit horizon). Before taking the number to committee, the desk wants
to see how FRAGILE that number is — how much it changes if WACC and g move even slightly
around the base case. It's the WACC × g sensitivity: a grid where each cell is a Terminal
Value recalculated for a different combination of the two assumptions.

*(This trainer doesn't generate the real Data Table in the sheet yet — the same limit already
seen in M0F-02: HyperFormula doesn't implement it. The exercise still trains exactly the
discipline that would make it work: a single formula, with three different anchors, copied across
the whole grid.)*

The Terminal Value for each combination is the Gordon perpetuity: **FCF × (1 + g) /
(WACC − g)**, where FCF is the (already normalised) FCF of the last explicit year. The rule
that holds the formula together is the same seen in Terminal Value: **WACC must always
stay above g**, otherwise the denominator collapses or flips sign — looking at
the grid, notice how quickly the value RISES as WACC falls towards g: that's exactly
why no real DCF trusts a single point.

**The data**, already set as assumptions: FCF of the last explicit year {p0}.
WACC goes from {p1} to {p2} in steps of 1 percentage
point, along the rows. g goes from {p3} to {p4} in steps
of 50 basis points, along the columns. The FCF sits in a single boxed cell: it's the number
every cell of the matrix must look at, never another place on the sheet.

After filling the grid, also compute its **range** (maximum minus minimum): it's the
number that answers the question "how sensitive is this valuation?" in a single
line.
